kf1.tip: Rank the three kashrut rules (permitted animals, shechita, separating milk and meat) by how hard each is to keep in a British school canteen, one line each.
kf1.note: Most would rank separating milk and meat hardest. It needs separate pots, plates, cutlery and surfaces, plus a waiting period, and a shared canteen kitchen rarely has these. Shechita comes next, because the meat must come from a trained shochet, so a pupil depends on certified food. Permitted animals is easiest, as you can simply avoid pork and shellfish. A weaker answer ranks the rules without tying each one to how a canteen works.

kf2.tip: Name the odd one out of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach, then justify it using what each festival remembers or asks of Jews.
kf2.note: Most would pick Pesach. It remembers a historical event, the Exodus from Egypt, and asks families to retell it at the Seder with symbolic foods. Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are linked by the Ten Days of Awe, and both ask Jews to reflect and repent. You could instead argue for Yom Kippur, the only one marked by a 25-hour fast rather than special food. A weaker answer names one without saying what each remembers or asks.

cs1.tip: Make the strongest case for the Orthodox view that kashrut is a mitzvah binding all Jews, then for Reform personal autonomy, then decide which convinces you.
cs1.note: A strong Orthodox case rests on the laws coming from the Torah. That makes them a divine mitzvah that binds every Jew, whether or not they understand the reason. The strongest Reform case is that kashrut matters for its meaning: identity, care in eating and discipline. So each person keeps it out of conviction. Either conclusion works if you weigh one against the other. The trap is only describing both views, or claiming Reform Jews reject kashrut, when some keep it fully.
